# Memory management: ARC, ORC, and `=destroy`

A program that allocates without ever cleaning up grows until it runs out of memory. In languages
with a garbage collector that is handled for you; in Nim 2.x the decision is made at compile time
through the memory mode. This chapter explains ARC and ORC, then the hooks the compiler calls at
the right moment: `=destroy`, `=copy`, and `=sink`.

::: {.callout-note}
## What you will be able to do

After this chapter you can explain how ARC and ORC differ, verify which memory mode is active, use
`--mm:arc` and `--mm:orc`, write `=destroy` for a type that owns a resource, and read the error for
a hook with the wrong signature.
:::

## Two memory modes: ARC and ORC

ARC and ORC both count references. Every time a `ref` is copied, the number of pointers goes up;
every time one disappears, it goes down. When that number reaches zero, the memory is freed right
then. There is no pause as with a classic garbage collector.

They differ in one thing: ORC adds cycle detection. Two objects pointing at each other never drop
to zero under plain counting; ORC finds such pairs and frees them. ARC does not, so cycles become
a memory leak.

That detection does not run all the time. ORC only sweeps for cycles after its internal list of roots
crosses a default threshold (128), or when `GC_fullCollect()` is called. In a small
program, cycles may still be alive when the program ends, so do not conclude from one short run
that ORC failed.

Since Nim 2.x the default mode is ORC.

## Checking which mode is active

The compiler defines symbols that can be tested with `when`.

```{.nim}
when defined(gcOrc):
  echo "orc"
elif defined(gcArc):
  echo "arc"
else:
  echo "other"
```

```{.txt}
orc
```

## Switching modes with `--mm`

To choose a different mode, pass a flag to the compiler. The example file `a06_mm_arc.nim` holds
the same code as above, with an `a06_mm_arc.mode` file containing `--mm:arc`. Run it with
`nim c -r --mm:arc main.nim`, and the output becomes `arc`, because the flag defines `gcArc`
instead of `gcOrc`. Change the flag to `--mm:orc` to return to the default mode. Verifying like
this is more convincing than memorizing which mode applies.

## `=destroy`: cleaning up when a value is dropped

When a type owns a resource outside managed memory, define `=destroy` so the resource is released.
Here is the order in which it is called.

```{.nim}
type Box = object
  name: string

proc `=destroy`(b: var Box) =
  echo "destroy ", b.name

proc make(): Box =
  echo "make"
  Box(name: "temp")

proc main() =
  var x = Box(name: "outer")
  echo "before block"
  block:
    let y = make()
    echo "inside block: ", y.name
  echo "after block"

main()
```

```{.txt}
before block
make
inside block: temp
destroy temp
after block
destroy outer
```

Read the order. `make()` prints `make`, then returns a `Box`; that value is stored in `y`. At the
end of the block, `y` leaves scope and `=destroy` is called for it, so `destroy temp` appears
before `after block`. `x` is only dropped at the end of `main()`, so `destroy outer` comes last.

## When the destructor is called

From the order above, the rule is clear:

- **End of scope.** `y` is dropped when its block ends, `x` when `main()` ends.
- **Temporary values.** Dropped no earlier than the end of the statement that uses them, and often
  only at the end of the enclosing scope. Do not rely on the exact moment.
- **Overwrite.** When a variable is overwritten, the old value is dropped first, unless its type has
  its own `=copy` or `=sink` hook: that hook is then responsible.

What does not happen: `=destroy` is not called the instant a value is created, and it is not
called for a `ptr` that points at the value.

## `=copy`: copying by your own rules

Copying from an existing location uses `=copy`.

```{.nim}
type Box = object
  name: string

proc `=copy`(dest: var Box; src: Box) =
  echo "copying ", src.name
  dest.name = src.name

var a = Box(name: "a")
var b = a
echo "b = ", b.name
```

```{.txt}
copying a
b = a
```

`var b = a` copies from a variable, so `=copy` is the one called. The definition above copies the
field shallowly. For a type that owns a file or a pointer, `=copy` must make a truly separate
copy, not duplicate the pointer.

The hook above also never frees the old value in `dest`. That is deliberate, to keep the example
short: once we write `=copy` ourselves, that responsibility moves to us. For resource-owning types,
start the hook with `=destroy(dest)`; otherwise the old resource leaks every time the value is
overwritten.

## `=sink`: absorbing a temporary

When the source is a temporary value that will not be used again, the compiler picks `=sink`
instead of `=copy`.

```{.nim}
type Box = object
  name: string

proc `=sink`(dest: var Box; src: Box) =
  echo "sinking ", src.name
  dest.name = src.name

var d = Box(name: "old")
d = Box(name: "temp")
echo "d = ", d.name
```

```{.txt}
sinking temp
d = temp
```

`Box(name: "temp")` is a temporary value; assigning it to `d` can move its contents, so `=sink` is
called. When the source is an ordinary variable, the path taken is `=copy`. Like `=copy`, this
hook takes over the duty of destroying the old value: `d` holds `old` before it is overwritten, and
the example above never calls `=destroy(dest)`, so a type that owns a resource has to add that call
itself.

## `move`: moving without hooks

`move` tells the compiler that the source may indeed be emptied.

```{.nim}
type Box = object
  name: string

var a = Box(name: "a")
var b = move(a)
echo "b = ", b.name
echo "a = ", repr(a.name)
```

```{.txt}
b = a
a = ""
```

`move(a)` moves the value without calling `=copy` or `=sink`, then empties `a` through `=wasMoved`;
a `string` goes back to `""`. After a `move`, the contents of `a` must not be relied on.

## Reading an error: a hook with the wrong signature

Every hook has a signature fixed by the compiler.

```{.nim}
type Box = object
  name: string

proc `=copy`(dest: var Box; src: string) =
  dest.name = src

var a = Box(name: "a")
var b = a
echo b.name
```

```{.txt}
main.nim(4, 1) Error: signature for '=copy' must be proc[T: object](x: var T; y: T)
```

The second parameter must have the same type as the value itself. The message spells out the
expected form completely: `proc[T: object](x: var T; y: T)`. Match the signature to that form.

## Rule of thumb

Leave the default hooks alone when a type only holds ordinary data; the compiler already provides
correct `=destroy`, `=copy`, and `=sink`. Write your own hooks only when the type owns a resource
outside managed memory, such as a file, a socket, or manually allocated memory.

## Exercises

Answers are in [Appendix A](../appendix/answers.qmd).

1. Write a type `Handle` with a `=destroy` that prints `close`; allocate one inside a block and
   note when the message appears.
2. Without running it, predict the output:
   ```{.nim}
   type Box = object
     name: string

   proc `=destroy`(b: var Box) =
     echo "drop ", b.name

   block:
     var a = Box(name: "a")
     echo "in block"
   echo "end"
   ```
3. Why does `move(a)` empty `a` but not call `=sink`?
4. Explain why ORC can free two objects pointing at each other, while ARC cannot.
5. The code below fails to compile. Fix it, then explain the error message:
   ```{.nim}
   type Person = ref object
     name: string

   proc `=destroy`(p: var Person) =
     echo "destroy ", p.name

   var x = Person(name: "a")
   echo x.name
   ```

## Summary

- Nim 2.x uses ORC by default; ARC is the same without cycle detection.
- `defined(gcOrc)` and `defined(gcArc)` detect the mode; `--mm:arc` and `--mm:orc` select it.
- `=destroy` is called at the end of scope, when a temporary is spent, and when a value is
  overwritten.
- `=copy` copies from a variable, `=sink` absorbs a temporary, and `move` moves without either.
- Write hooks only when a type owns a resource outside managed memory.
